session: Session 1 - Introduction: populations, samples and variables
bullets: Descriptive statistics summarise and organise data (mean, median, mode, standard deviation, charts) to answer business questions.
Cases (rows) are the objects studied; variables (columns) are characteristics; an identifier variable uniquely identifies each case.
Categorical variables: nominal (order does not matter, e.g. payment method) or ordinal (order matters, e.g. satisfaction). Quantitative: discrete (counts) or continuous (measured, e.g. commute time).
Population vs sample; parameter (describes the population, usually unknown) vs statistic (calculated from a sample to estimate it). Vegan study: 61 of 865 gives statistic 7.05%.
Good samples are representative, randomly selected and large enough. Larger samples tend to have smaller sampling error.
Random methods: simple random, systematic (every nth), stratified (random sample from each subgroup), cluster (random clusters, sample all members).
Bias: sampling bias, nonresponse bias, response bias. A sampling frame is the list from which the sample is drawn.
Bad survey questions: double-barrelled, ambiguous word, leading, odd-point scale that invites the middle, overlapping answer ranges (use 18-29, 30-39).
examTip: Identify population, sample, parameter and statistic in a scenario, and classify variables correctly (discrete vs continuous, nominal vs ordinal).

session: Session 2 - Displaying and describing categorical data
bullets: Count = number in a category; proportion = count / total (between 0 and 1); percentage = proportion × 100%. Population proportion p, sample proportion p̂.
Frequency table (counts) and relative frequency table (proportions or percentages that sum to 1 or 100%).
Example: 526 of 832 chose Netflix gives p̂ = 0.632 (63.2%).
Pie chart: slices show how a whole is split; categories cannot overlap and it gets messy beyond about six categories. Bar graph: counts or proportions, works with overlap (continents visited).
Contingency table compares two categorical variables; the response variable is what you measure, the explanatory variable may explain it.
Marginal distribution: totals in the margins. Conditional distribution: cell count divided by the total of the explanatory category.
Compare conditional percentages, not raw counts: second-year 54.49% vs third-year 72.39% have a job; small samples (53 fourth-years) limit conclusions.
Independent variables show no relationship (similar conditional percentages). Show with side-by-side or segmented (stacked) bar graphs.
examTip: Always divide by the explanatory category total to get the conditional distribution; do not read conclusions from raw counts.

session: Session 3 - Quantitative data part I: shape, mean, standard deviation
bullets: Describe a quantitative variable by shape, center and spread.

Histogram: split the range into bins, count observations per bin, bar height = count. Shapes: symmetric, uniform, unimodal, skewed (right-skewed has a few unusually large values), normal (symmetric and bell-shaped).
Cumulative frequency table: running total of frequencies; also cumulative relative frequency.
Mean = sum / n. For grouped data use interval midpoints × frequencies. Sample std s uses the n − 1 divisor; variance is s squared (squared units, so use std).
Example: monthly profits 65, 70, 78, 81, 89, 97 give mean 80 and s ≈ 11.8. Within 1 std is common; beyond 3 std is highly unusual.
Multiply every value by a: mean and std multiply by a. Add a: mean shifts by a, std unchanged.
Coefficient of variation = s / mean (percent); above 30% means heterogeneous; used to compare different scales.
Z-score = (x − mean)/s. Outlier rule 1: more than 3 std from the mean. Mean and std are sensitive to extremes: use for symmetric data.
examTip: Compare across scales with z-scores (e.g. 93 on a 90/10 exam is z = 0.3), and remember the sample std divides by n − 1.

session: Session 4 - Quantitative data part II: percentiles, IQR and boxplots
bullets: Percentile q_a: value at or below which a×100 percent of values fall. Position = a × n; if not an integer round up and take that ordered value. Deciles and quartiles are special percentiles.
Median Q2: odd n takes the middle value; even n averages the two middle values (77 and 78 give 77.5).
Example (n = 20 wages): Q1 = 66 (0.25 × 20 = 5th value), Q3 = 84 (15th value).
Range = max − min (sensitive to one extreme value). IQR = Q3 − Q1: spread of the middle 50%.
Outlier rule 2: below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. With IQR 18: cutoffs 39 and 111, so 32 is an outlier.
Median and IQR are resistant; mean, std and range are sensitive. Replacing an outlier lowers std, median unchanged.
Five number summary: min, Q1, median, Q3, max. Boxplot: box from Q1 to Q3, line at median, whiskers to the largest and smallest non-outliers, outliers marked with asterisks.
For grouped continuous data find the percentile by locating the class where the cumulative proportion passes a, then interpolate linearly (q0.25 ≈ 6.05).
examTip: Use median and IQR for skewed data or data with outliers, and apply the 1.5 × IQR fences from Q1 and Q3.

session: Session 5 - Exploring relationships: covariance, correlation and regression
bullets: Review problem: income x and consumption y; given Σ(x − x̄)², Σ(y − ȳ)² and Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ), compute means, variances and covariance from them.
Sample variance s²x = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1); sample covariance s_xy = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ)/(n − 1).
Correlation r = s_xy / (s_x · s_y). Example r ≈ 0.9979: very strong positive linear relationship, logical since richer households consume more.
Regression line of y on x: slope b1 = s_xy / s²x, intercept b0 = ȳ − b1·x̄. Example b1 ≈ 0.7810, b0 ≈ 1,176.
Coefficient of determination R² = r² (simple regression with a constant): share of the variability in y explained by x. Example 99.58%.
Forecast: ŷ = b0 + b1·x; income 16,800 gives about 14,297. High R² makes forecasts reasonably reliable.
Syllabus also lists correlation vs causation: a strong correlation alone does not prove one variable causes the other.
examTip: Follow the sequence: means, variances, covariance, r, then b1 and b0, R² = r²; and comment on reliability, not just the number.
